title: How can sixty degree steps build a bigger angle?
description: A line with a point A on it, and three arcs of one radius stepping round A. Two equilateral triangles sit side by side, and their angles at A add up to the angle we want. Keeko's doubt, cutting from the same point twice, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: each arc step of the same radius adds another sixty degrees at A. Watch for students who cut again from the old point instead of the new one.

source: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a
video_script.why: The child builds a larger angle by adding two equal sixty degree steps.
video_script.substitution: Each new arc of the same radius, centred on the last point, adds another equilateral triangle at A.
video_script.anchor: A line with the point A marked on it and X to the right of A.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko cuts the arc from B again for the second step. The compass lands on C once more, so the angle stays sixty degrees.
video_script.payoff_line: Angle D eigh X is one hundred and twenty degrees.

final_answer.spoken: angle D eigh X is one hundred and twenty degrees

maths_rules: Centre A, any radius, cut AX at B. Centre B, same radius, cut the arc at C. Triangle ABC is equilateral, so ∠CAB = 60°.
Centre C, same radius, cut the arc at D. Triangle ACD is equilateral, so ∠DAC = 60°.
Check: 180° − (60° + 60°) = 60° is left on the other side of AD.
Slip: cutting from B again lands on C, so the angle stays 60°.
video_script.design: One line, one point A and one compass opening. Three arcs step round A, two triangles are shaded. The slip is the second cut from the old point.
